RESEARCH ASSESSMENT · Literature cutoff: October 19, 2026 · local audit and source inspection

Which medical claims are justified by the evidence the model actually receives?

The information-gap framework is reasonable and worth discussing with your advisor. The evidence supports a concrete supervision problem and a testable research program. It does not yet establish a dominant root cause of medical MLLM failure.

JudgmentPaper evidenceLocal auditData examplesExisting pilotsTheoryDecisive studyFiles and reproduction

Presentation PDF · Editable PowerPoint · Evidence CSV · Case CSV · Full case manifest

Suggested thesis. Some medical training targets combine visible observations with facts supplied only to the annotator or synthetic teacher. Explicitly matching each claim to its available evidence may reduce unsupported assertions while retaining useful medical knowledge and diagnostic performance.

Assessment of the discussion notes

Notes claimJudgmentRevision for the advisor
Bidirectional image–text gapAgree as an organizing frameworkSeparate unavailable patient facts, omitted visible findings, ambiguous findings, and available-but-unused evidence. They need different labels and experiments.
More data mainly improves language; scaling does little for evidenceToo strongLingshu and Huatuo report gains; MedGemma 1.5 expands evidence access. Test whether scaling alone leaves specific unsupported-claim rates unresolved, at matched data quality. [P02–P04]
MLE on image-only reports encourages unsupported contentPlausible; concrete cases existA Bayes-optimal conditional distribution can marginalize missing context honestly. MLE does not mathematically force fabrication; deterministic reporting and answer-only evaluation can incentivize over-specific assertions.
Unreported content gets no gradientLiteral wording is wrongThere is no direct target naming that content, but shared visual features, other captions and previous training supply indirect learning. A coverage deficit needs independent image labels.
Teacher captions are mostly off-image; mixing necessarily shrinks overlapNot measuredSource rankings in the notes are qualitative hypotheses. Mixture entropy and usable-information ratios are not monotonic in source size; answerability must be audited per source.
Frozen representations bound downstream recoveryAgree with conditionsThe limitation is about a fixed input/representation, not the calendar stage called post-training. Encoder updates, crops, additional views and tools change the information available.
A failed probe means pretraining is neededDisagree as a decision ruleProbe failure may reflect sample size, pooling or predictor capacity. Successful decoding also does not prove causal use of a lesion. Interventions are needed.
Counterfactual tests and provenance are preferable to hedging rateAgree; strong directionRequire appropriate changes after relevant evidence changes, and stability after irrelevant changes. Preserve performance on answerable cases. Very close methods already exist. [P15,P19–P22]
No current signal rewards grounding or uncertaintyIncorrect as a universal claimMCR, RadVLM, RULE, MedReasoner and CARE-MVLM already address aspects of these objectives. The remaining claim must be narrower.
Medical dense recaptioning cannot transferToo absoluteRoI- and mask-based medical supervision already exists. Its cost, coverage and independent reliability remain constraints, rather than a proof of impossibility.
Typed uncertainty follows automatically from PVINot establishedAblation scores measure model/intervention dependence. They do not label why evidence is insufficient; experts or structural evidence labels are still needed.
All three failures share one demonstrated causeNot establishedMissing context is a shared candidate mechanism. Resolution, acquisition, disease ambiguity, prevalence, label noise and deployment shift remain competing or interacting causes.

Repair the interpretation of the notes’ cited evidence

Citation in notesWhat it can supportWhat to avoid
[1] MIRAGE via the 3D oncology paperCite MIRAGE directly [P13]; the oncology preprint is a useful separate private-data study.Conflating private data with guaranteed visual dependence; text cues can remain. Oncology source.
[2] RadImageNet-VQAText-only performance depends on benchmark and question format [P14].Calling 2–10% open-ended accuracy a mathematically defined chance level.

[4] Lingshu physician agreement36% exact rating agreement, 81% within one point, weighted kappa 0.64 [P03].Interpreting exact ordinal-score disagreement as evidence that 64% of diagnostic ground truths are unreliable.

Evidence from backbones and medical reasoning papers

Rows distinguish an author-reported result from our interpretation. Follow the linked primary source and locator for the exact protocol. This is a targeted review, not an exhaustive systematic review. Scores from different papers are not directly comparable.

P01 · mechanism

LLaVA-Med

NeurIPS 2023 · Read: Section 3; figure-caption and inline-mention instruction construction

Reported evidence: GPT-4 builds instructions from figure captions and, in 60K-IM, article sentences mentioning the figure. The instruction teacher does not inspect pixels.

Interpretation: Teacher-side article knowledge can enter targets even when the student receives only a figure and question.

Boundary: A privileged teacher is not intrinsically defective; inspect each target for answerability. Local training-data directories are empty, so no local LLaVA-Med QA prevalence is claimed.

P02 · mechanism and counterevidence

HuatuoGPT-Vision / PubMedVision

EMNLP 2024 · Read: Section 2; Table 2; Appendix H; arXiv:2406.19280v2

Reported evidence: GPT-4V sees both image and source text during reformatting. PubMedVision totals about 1.3M alignment/instruction entries. On the paper's shared LLaVA-8B setup, adding PubMedVision increases average medical VQA accuracy from 51.0 to 62.7.

Interpretation: Image-aware denoising improves performance while leaving a testable question about information retained from captions.

Boundary: Do not describe this as a text-only teacher or imply that its quality controls are absent. Its limitations explicitly acknowledge synthetic hallucinations.

P03 · mechanism and mixed outcomes

Lingshu / Lingshu-Med

2025; v5 September 2026, TPAMI acceptance stated · Read: II-B1, II-B4; V-E/Table IV; V-F; Appendix F

Reported evidence: Caption generation uses RoIs, metadata and medical knowledge; reasoning distillation supplies the known answer. RL changes the reported seven-task average from 61.8 to 61.5. Physician-rating exact agreement is 36%, within-one-point agreement 81%, and weighted kappa averages 0.64.

Interpretation: Supports auditing visual premises independently of answer-conditioned rationales and headline averages.

Boundary: These are rating agreements, not disagreement about patient truth. Lingshu actively improves data quality and reports scaling benefits; it is not evidence that scaling cannot improve perception.

P04 · counterevidence

MedGemma 1.5 Technical Report

April 2026 preprint · Read: Sections 2.2–2.3; multi-timepoint and volumetric evaluations

Reported evidence: Adds volumetric CT/MRI, whole-slide inputs, bounding-box localization and multi-timepoint CXR analysis. Volumetric prompts include report indications; up to 85 axial slices are processed.

Interpretation: Supplying context and improving input coverage already form part of strong backbone development.

Boundary: Counters blanket claims that current systems only scale report text or cannot handle longitudinal evidence. Improved task scores alone still do not validate every generated claim.

P05 · external clinical evidence

Comparative evaluation of generative AI models for CXR report generation in the ED

European Radiology, June 2026 · Read: Methods; Table 2; finding-level CT-referenced analysis

Reported evidence: In 478 selected ED patients with same-day CT, Lingshu had RADPEER 3b ratings in 616/1434 reads (43.0%) versus radiologists' 200/1434 (13.9%), while clarity was 88.0% versus 78.1%. AIRead had a 5.3% RADPEER 3b rate.

Interpretation: Fluent reporting and diagnostic quality can diverge markedly.

Boundary: 1434 is 478 cases times three readers, not independent patients. This single-center, CT-selected cohort cannot identify training-objective causality or establish a general model ranking.

P06 · direct precedent

Removing hallucinated references to non-existent priors

ML4H 2022 · Read: Methods; MIMIC-CXR rewriting and CXR-ReDonE experiments

Reported evidence: Identifies prior-comparison targets in single-study report generation and retrains on reports with those references removed or rewritten.

Interpretation: A direct medical precedent for supervision that requires unavailable evidence, plus an intervention on that supervision.

Boundary: This already establishes the missing-prior case. A new project must extend beyond rediscovering it, and preserve current findings while removing comparisons.

P07 · direct intervention and novelty constraint

DPO for suppressing hallucinated prior exams

2024 preprint · Read: Section 5.2/Table 1; Section 5.3/Table 2

Reported evidence: A tested DPO setting reduces reports mentioning priors from 51.63% to 20.90%; clinical metrics show tradeoffs and SFT can perform better.

Interpretation: Post-training can modify unsupported attribution, but suppression must be assessed alongside retained clinical accuracy.

Boundary: Prior-reference removal, DPO, and safety–utility tradeoffs are established prior art.

P08 · reasoning baseline

MedVLM-R1

MICCAI 2025 · Read: Method/format and accuracy rewards; abstract and main evaluation

Reported evidence: GRPO with 600 training VQA examples reports average accuracy increasing from 55.11% to 78.22%. Reasoning references are not required; rewards evaluate final-answer correctness and output format.

Interpretation: A useful positive result for RL efficiency, but a correct final answer does not independently validate the intermediate visual premises.

Boundary: These protocol-specific scores should not be compared numerically with other papers' averages. The reward design alone does not prove hallucinated reasoning.

P09 · reasoning baseline

Med-R1

March 2025, version 1 · Read: Methods; GRPO reward design and eight-modality evaluation

Reported evidence: Uses GRPO with answer/format rewards across eight imaging modalities and reports gains over its Qwen2-VL-2B base.

Interpretation: Tests generalization over modalities and tasks, providing a stronger comparator than a single VQA dataset.

Boundary: Answer accuracy and interpretable-looking traces do not establish evidence sufficiency. Later versions change the base model; version-specific numbers must not be mixed.

P10 · reasoning baseline

GMAI-VL-R1

April 2025 preprint · Read: Reasoning synthesis, rejection sampling, and RL method

Reported evidence: Combines synthesized reasoning, rejection sampling and reinforcement learning for multimodal medical diagnosis and VQA.

Interpretation: Adds a broad medical reasoning comparator to answer-only and distilled-CoT baselines.

Boundary: Accepting an answer-correct trajectory does not certify each observation. A causal audit is needed before attributing its gains to improved visual grounding.

P11 · support with alternative explanations

MedVLThinker

August 2025 preprint · Read: Training comparisons; text-only versus image-text RLVR

Reported evidence: Curated text-only RLVR gives larger gains on the tested public medical VQA benchmarks than the tested multimodal training recipe.

Interpretation: Medical VQA improvement can come from reasoning or language adaptation without new medical images.

Boundary: Different training-data quality is a confound. This result does not mean the image is unused at inference or that medical vision training is generally unhelpful.

P12 · direct evaluation precedent

Beyond Accuracy: Evaluating Visual Grounding in Multimodal Medical Reasoning

March 2026 preprint · Read: Sections 3.2–3.5; Tables 1–4

Reported evidence: On 100 items each from four benchmarks, image-text RL changes accuracy from 56.5% to 58.8% while image sensitivity falls from 48.2% to 39.8%. The PathVQA negative VRS estimate has a confidence interval crossing zero.

Interpretation: Direct evidence that answer scores and image-intervention metrics can diverge; a close evaluation predecessor.

Boundary: Random shuffling can preserve a correct label. Answer invariance plus visual wording is not sufficient to label an individual claim false. The small preprint study is suggestive, not a universal RL result.

P13 · direct evaluation precedent

MIRAGE: The Illusion of Visual Understanding

March/April 2026 preprint, v2 · Read: No-image versus explicit-guessing experiments; B-Clean

Reported evidence: Models produce visual descriptions without images, and some medical benchmark performance remains high. Explicit guessing instructions can change results substantially.

Interpretation: An absent-image control is necessary, with prompts and failure handling specified.

Boundary: Does not distinguish benchmark contamination, question cues and legitimate medical knowledge by itself. Blank images, omitted images and corrupted images are different interventions.

P14 · benchmark evidence and counterexample

RadImageNet-VQA

December 2025; March 2026 v2 · Read: Figure 4; text-only analysis

Reported evidence: Text-only open-ended VQA-RAD/SLAKE accuracy spans about 11.5–33% in the tested models, while the new benchmark has much lower text-only performance. Four-choice text-only results on the new benchmark lie near 25%.

Interpretation: Benchmark construction can reduce exploitable text cues.

Boundary: Open-ended 'chance' is not well defined. Low performance for a few text-only models does not prove complete freedom from all shortcuts or contamination.

P15 · close methodological predecessor

Act as You Think / Multi-Consistency Reward

ACL July 2026 · Read: Section 3.4; perceptual and reasoning consistency rewards; Tables 6–8

Reported evidence: Med-Zero-17K and MCR explicitly address visual/reasoning/answer inconsistency. Training rewards include image-corruption behavior and reasoning–answer coherence.

Interpretation: Grounding-aware RL is already established; compare against it directly.

Boundary: A text coherence judge or sensitivity to broad image corruption does not by itself verify a specific lesion premise. Consistency can coexist with a false premise.

P16 · counterevidence and method comparator

RadVLM with RL for reporting and grounding

December 2025 preprint · Read: Matched thinking/non-thinking and RL experiments

Reported evidence: Task-specific RL improves report generation and visual grounding, while adding explicit thinking does not consistently help.

Interpretation: Counters claims that all existing rewards only measure language or that longer reasoning is necessarily beneficial.

Boundary: Grounding and report metrics do not guarantee sufficiency of all diagnostic claims; compare with matched evidence access and training budgets.

P17 · specific supervision mechanism

ChestX-Reasoner: step-by-step verification from daily reports

Communications Medicine, May 2026 · Read: Methods: RadRScore and RadRBench-CXR; mining reasoning chains

Reported evidence: Mines reasoning from reports and uses report-based process rewards. Its construction treats an unmentioned finding as normal/no disease under an explicit completeness assumption.

Interpretation: A concrete instance where report omissions can become negative reasoning supervision, making an independent image audit valuable.

Boundary: An exposed assumption is not proof of an actual wrong label. The work includes clinical evaluation and useful gains; the next test is whether the omitted finding is present on the supplied image.

P18 · counterevidence and comparator

MedReasoner

AAAI 2026; 2025 preprint · Read: UMRG/U-MRG-14K; reasoner and frozen segmentation expert

Reported evidence: Pairs implicit clinical queries and reasoning with pixel masks; RL trains a reasoner that prompts a frozen segmentation expert.

Interpretation: Dense medical visual supervision and reasoning-grounding integration are feasible in bounded tasks.

Boundary: Segmentation success is not a complete certificate of diagnostic reasoning, but it contradicts an absolute claim that dense medical supervision cannot transfer.

P19 · close methodological predecessor

Med-OPD

July 2026 preprint · Read: Sections 3.2–3.5; image-degradation token weights; Table 1

Reported evidence: Weights answer-aware teacher tokens by positive original-versus-low-resolution likelihood differences; reports 0.7058 average versus 0.6775 for OPD on the tested subsets.

Interpretation: Counterfactual image-conditioned token weighting is already close prior art.

Boundary: Teacher dependence on broad image degradation is a model-specific proxy, not a ground-truth sufficiency label.

P20 · close conceptual predecessor

MedTRACE

September 2026 preprint; ADMA acceptance stated · Read: Sections 3.1–3.5; Section 4.2 metric definitions

Reported evidence: Explicitly models evidence sufficiency, acquisition tools, verification, memory and confidence. Its unsupported-error metric requires an incorrect diagnosis and evidence not matching expert support.

Interpretation: An evidence ledger, acquisition policy or sufficiency score alone is not a new contribution.

Boundary: Correct diagnoses with false visual premises require a separate audit, as do source-derived claims that are not supplied to the student.

P21 · close methodological predecessor

Spatial and factual RL for CXR reporting

September 2026 preprint · Read: Equation 5; spatial/factual ablations and reward hacking analysis

Reported evidence: Uses regions and boxes with a spatial IoU gate before factual reward, and documents reward hacking.

Interpretation: Joint spatial/factual process rewards are existing work; reference-report correctness remains a supervision assumption to audit.

Boundary: An anatomical box is not necessarily a lesion-specific causal explanation. An audit must test the claim's actual evidence requirement.

P22 · closest recent counterfactual predecessor

CARE-MVLM

September 2026 medRxiv preprint · Read: Counterfactual view construction; answerability selector; 7358 triplets

Reported evidence: Uses original, lesion-removed and matched random-removal mammograms to train grounding and abstention behavior, with a separate answerability selector.

Interpretation: Clinically targeted lesion removal plus an unrelated-region control is already very close prior art.

Boundary: Editing artifacts and the equivalence between removal and answer unavailability need validation. Extend to source provenance and missing clinical context rather than claiming lesion-removal novelty.

P23 · uncertainty and context predecessor

RULE

EMNLP 2024 · Read: Calibrated retrieval-size selection and preference tuning

Reported evidence: Controls factuality risk when selecting retrieved context and uses preferences to correct over-reliance on retrieval.

Interpretation: Risk calibration and balancing context use already have medical multimodal precedents.

Boundary: Retrieved medical references are not the same as patient-specific evidence. Useful knowledge should remain available while unsupported patient facts are withheld.

P24 · process evaluation precedent

MedBench v5

June 2026 preprint · Read: Dynamic audit construction; information omission/contradiction/delay; judge validation

Reported evidence: Uses 90 base instances expanded into 720 stress scenarios and audits diagnosis updates and evidence handling. Reported answer–reference judge validation has weighted kappa 0.32.

Interpretation: Supports evaluating evidence arrival and revision, beyond final answers.

Boundary: 720 variants are not 720 independent patients; the reported judge validation does not establish expert validity for every dynamic-node label.

P25 · weak illustrative evidence

Wound-image evaluation of HuluMed, MedGemma and chatbots

June 2026 preprint · Read: Scoring framework and limitations, 20 cases

Reported evidence: Reports noncommittal outputs on a small wound-image set. The scoring rule automatically treats substantial hedging or structural ambiguity as incorrect.

Interpretation: Illustrates an actionability concern and the need to inspect uncertainty policies.

Boundary: The rubric penalizes hedging by construction; this is not direct evidence of miscalibration, nor a controlled test of the proposed information-gap mechanism.

T01 · theory boundary

V-usable information and pointwise V-information

ICLR 2020 / ICML 2022 · Read: PVI construction; defined predictor families and fitted null/input predictors

Reported evidence: PVI evaluates instance difficulty relative to a predictor family and data distribution; usable information can change under computation.

Interpretation: Fit comparable input and null predictors on training data and validate on held-out cases before claiming a usable-information estimate.

Boundary: A frozen model's image-ablation gain is not Shannon MI, an expert sufficiency label, or an estimator of each entropy term.

T02 · theory boundary

Conformal Risk Control

ICLR 2024 · Read: Main theorem; bounded monotone loss family

Reported evidence: Controls expected loss under the procedure's assumptions and calibration design.

Interpretation: Define the clinical loss and nested output family before calibrating; a better score can improve efficiency.

Boundary: Expected population risk is not a per-patient promise, and standard CRC does not automatically control selective risk among non-abstained cases. A few hundred cases may be inadequate for rare-finding groups.

T03 · theory boundary

Language Models with Conformal Factuality Guarantees

ICML 2024 · Read: Entailment sets and nested back-off construction

Reported evidence: Connects factuality to conformal prediction using less-specific outputs and calibration labels.

Interpretation: A valid claim-filtering/back-off system requires appropriate labels and a precisely defined guarantee.

Boundary: A report omission is not a truth label; generic claim filtering is not automatically covered by the theorem, and hospital shift can break exchangeability.

Where a new contribution could remain

MIRAGE and Beyond Accuracy already challenge image dependence. MCR and Med-OPD already use image-conditioned reward signals. CARE-MVLM already uses lesion removal, matched random removal and abstention. MedTRACE already models evidence sufficiency and acquisition. A defensible candidate contribution is a claim-level audit and controlled intervention on teacher-only patient facts and missing panels, evaluated on correct-answer/false-premise cases as well as incorrect diagnoses. Claim novelty only after a broader overlap check.

What the local data actually show

The scripts scan local files read-only and save checksums. Counts describe these copies and task wrappers, not the complete published datasets. Multiple records can belong to one patient or figure. Keyword matches are screening flags, not clinical error labels.

The explicit screen looks for phrases such as “compared with,” “in comparison with,” and “previous study.” The broader screen also includes “stable,” “unchanged” and follow-up wording. Neither count asserts that every matched sentence is false. In these wrappers, no prior image, report or history is provided in the prompt; inspect the exact target before editing.

Image OCR, the identity of the patient referenced, hypothetical examples and approximate-age questions are not adjudicated by the age count. The 993 count is therefore neither a clinical hallucination rate nor a lower bound on one. A uniform 4,000-record reservoir is saved for independent annotation; keyword-selected examples are illustrative.

Benchmark controls fitted without images

SLAKE English baselineTest exact match95% image-cluster bootstrap interval
Global train answer mode175/1061 = 16.5%14.8%–18.1%
Train mode by content-type metadata306/1061 = 28.8%26.0%–31.7%
Exact normalized train-question lookup; global fallback579/1061 = 54.6%51.7%–57.2%

Train: 4,919 English QA over 450 images. Test: 1,061 QA over 96 images. Image overlap is zero. Of test questions, 999 have an exact normalized question in train; answers are selected using train frequencies only. Question lookup gets 494/913 on the designated visual-QA subset and 87/148 on knowledge QA under the metadata-fallback variant. Repeated templates and answer frequency explain useful baseline performance without proving any particular image claim unsupported. These are new lookup results, not medical MLLM scores.

On PMC-VQA, the most frequent training answer letter is B. Predicting B blindly gives 15,854/50,000 = 31.708%, compared with a nominal four-option random baseline of 25%. The local files contain 14 malformed train labels and 10 malformed test labels; this raw-file denominator includes them. Option balancing and shuffling are necessary controls, but this result does not establish image independence for individual questions.

The local VQA-RAD file named MED_RAD_test.json contains 2,248 rows over 314 images, resembling the full original corpus rather than a verified held-out split. Its CLOSED metadata also includes non-binary answers. Do not infer published test scores or assume all CLOSED questions are yes/no. The LLaVA-Med code checkout exists, but the expected data/instruct and data/pmc_articles training directories are empty; this review makes no local training-example claim for that dataset.

Eleven traceable examples, including controls

Full original QA, captions, file paths and intervention suggestions are in the manifest. Labels below concern structural evidence availability; subtle image findings and diagnostic appropriateness still need specialist adjudication. No new patient-specific medical advice is implied.

C01 · PubMedVision · missing patient-specific test result

Biopsy confirmation in an MRI-only answer

Record Instruction-Tuning_422538 · Figure 5

Question: I noticed the mass in the image seems quite large and different in texture. Does this indicate something malignant or harmful?

Assessment: The answer asserts that biopsy results confirmed the diagnosis. Only a breast MR image and a concern about the mass are supplied. The published source caption separately reports the biopsy.

Aligned target behavior: Describe the supplied image; distinguish a differential from biopsy confirmation. State that the biopsy result was not supplied.

Discriminating test: Add or withhold the actual biopsy report; test whether confirmation language changes while visual description remains stable.

Original article / figure attribution

Inspect exact target, caption, and local provenance

Original answer: It's understandable to be concerned about the appearance of the mass. However, the detailed characteristics you notice in the MRI, such as the well-defined borders and the internal structure, are typical of a fibroadenoma, especially with lactational changes in a breastfeeding patient. Fibroadenomas are benign breast tumors, meaning they are not cancerous. They can change in size and feel during hormonal changes like pregnancy or lactation. The size and texture changes you see are expected under these conditions, and it doesn't usually indicate malignancy. Our biopsy results confirm this diagnosis, which helps us ensure accurate treatment and monitoring.

Original caption: A 34-year-old lactating patient complained of a rapidly growing mass in the left breast. T2 (A) and post-contrast T1 (B) weighted MRI images showed a complex solid and cystic mass in the upper quadrants of the left breast, in the same topography of a previous biopsy compatible with fibroadenoma. A new percutaneous biopsy confirmed the diagnosis of fibroadenoma with lactational changes.

C02 · PubMedVision · missing patient-specific test result

CT morphology and a histology event

Record Instruction-Tuning_141171 · Figure 1

Question: What is the likely diagnosis based on the findings in this CT scan?

Assessment: The CT may support a malignant differential, but it does not establish that a CT-guided biopsy was performed or what histology it returned.

Aligned target behavior: Describe cavitary morphology and a differential; attribute a confirmed subtype only when the histology result is supplied.

Discriminating test: Supply a pathology result with an alternative subtype; evaluate appropriate attribution rather than requiring CT appearance to change.

Original article / figure attribution

Inspect exact target, caption, and local provenance

Original answer: Based on the findings in the CT scan, the likely diagnosis is non-small cell lung adenocarcinoma. The presence of a cavitary lesion with an irregular and thick wall is a characteristic feature of lung cancer, particularly adenocarcinoma. The reference information provided indicates that a CT-guided biopsy was performed, and the histological evaluation confirmed the diagnosis of non-small cell adenocarcinoma. Lung cancer can present with a variety of radiographic findings, including cavitary lesions, and the CT features in this case are highly suggestive of a malignant process.

Original caption: Axial CT scan at the level of the upper lobes with a lung window setting showing a cavitary lesion with an irregular and thick wall. A CT-guided biopsy was taken from the thick wall, and histological evaluation confirmed non-small cell adenocarcinoma.

C03 · PubMedVision · missing patient-specific test result

Suspicion on MRI versus confirmed invasion

Record Instruction-Tuning_572961 · Figure 13

Question: What is the main pathological finding observed in this medical image?

Assessment: The source distinguishes an MRI appearance suspicious for invasion from subsequent histopathological confirmation. The student answer combines them without access to pathology.

Aligned target behavior: Keep image-supported suspicion separate from histological confirmation.

Discriminating test: Withhold/add the pathology report; score the confirmed-event claim separately from the visible finding.

Original article / figure attribution

Inspect exact target, caption, and local provenance

Original answer: The main pathological finding observed in this medical image is the presence of an intraocular enhancing retinoblastoma combined with focal choroidal thickening and a discontinuity of the normal choroidal enhancement pattern adjacent to the tumor mass. This discontinuity of the normal choroidal enhancement is a leading criterion for indicating tumor invasion, as confirmed by the histopathological examination of the eye, which showed massive choroidal invasion.

Original caption: Postcontrast transaxial T1-weighted (TR/TE, 305/15 ms) MRI. Intraocular enhancing retinoblastoma combined with focal choroidal thickening and a discontinuity of the linear enhancement pattern of the choroid (arrowheads) adjacent to the tumor mass is suspicious for tumor invasion. Histopathological examination of this eye showed massive choroidal invasion

C04 · PubMedVision · missing image panel and treatment details

A caption references a perfusion panel absent from the supplied image

Record Instruction-Tuning_544331 · Figure 1(a,b)

Question: As an intern, I noticed an irregular enhancement in the left insular cortex on this MRI. Can you explain what this might indicate in the context of breast cancer metastasis and follow-up treatment?

Assessment: The supplied file shows one structural MR view. The source caption describes both structural panel (a) and perfusion panel (b); the answer asserts increased rCBV and a 20 Gy treatment dose. Neither is supplied in the question.

Aligned target behavior: Discuss the visible enhancement with uncertainty; request perfusion data for the rCBV claim and history for treatment timing/dose.

Discriminating test: Present structural image alone versus structural plus original perfusion panel; independently add the treatment history.

Original article / figure attribution

Inspect exact target, caption, and local provenance

Original answer: This irregular enhancement in the left insular cortex is highly suggestive of a recurrence of breast cancer metastasis, particularly when noted one year after stereotactic radiosurgery (SRS) treatment with a dose of 20 Gy. The enhanced area likely represents in-field recurrence where the original breast cancer metastasis was treated. The increased relative cerebral blood volume (rCBV) in the perfusion study, as seen in this MRI scan, likely indicates neo-angiogenesis, which is a process of new blood vessel formation commonly associated with tumor growth. This new vessel formation increases the blood volume feeding the tumor, contributing to its growth and progression. This scenario requires prompt confirmation via further diagnostic procedures, like a biopsy, followed by therapeutic adjustment which might include more targeted radiotherapy or chemotherapy to manage disease progression.

Original caption: (a) Contrast enhanced T1-weighted magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) showing a suspected in-field recurrence one year after SRS (20 Gy) for a breast cancer metastasis in the left insular cortex; (b) the perfusion study is suggestive of disease progression because of relative cerebral blood volume (rCBV) increase due to the neo-angiogenesis within the insular cortex tissue.

Inspect exact target, caption, and local provenance

Original answer: The MRI scans show bone marrow edema-like changes in the patella area of the knee, which is often seen after increased physical activity, such as running a marathon. For the right knee (31-year-old woman), there's been some improvement in the edema but not a complete return to the initial state before the marathon. This suggests that some residual inflammation or stress response is still present. For the left knee (34-year-old woman), the edema has completely resolved, which is excellent news. Typically, treatment for bone marrow edema would include rest, avoiding strenuous activity, possibly ice and anti-inflammatory medications. It's also important to gradually increase knee-loading activities to allow the knee to adapt without overwhelming it. Recovery can vary by individual, but with appropriate management, most people see improvements.

Original caption: Axial proton-density fat-saturated MR images of two different knees that showed reversibility at 6-month follow-up (MRI 3) in the extent of subchondral bone marrow oedema-like signal of the patella that previously developed from the pre-marathon scan to the 2 weeks post-marathon scan (MRI 1 to MRI 2): A) reversibility but not to the MRI 1 grading status, in the right knee of a 31-year old woman; B) complete resolution to the MRI 1 grading status, in the left knee of a 34-year-old woman. Bone marrow oedema-like signal is indicated by arrows and the lesion grade (G) is included in the left bottom corner and is defined in the KOSS scoring system [18] (see Table 2); KOSS, Knee Osteoarthritis Scoring System

What the existing workspace pilots add

These runs predate this review. I inspected archived raw-choice files, result summaries, checkpoints and protocols; I did not rerun GPU inference. They are exploratory, use selected cases, and are not independent evidence of population prevalence.

The 96-record evidence-mismatch pilot uses 32 examples in each of external-context, diagnostic-inference and visual-description strata. Both tested checkpoints show lower image-identity gain and greater caption specificity for the external-context targets. This is consistent with model dependence on source information. Differences in claim content and selection remain confounds, and caption rescue can partly expose the answer directly.

The follow-up uses 12 reviewed external facts, plus 12 broad-anatomy images (six head/chest pairs). A provenance prompt increases missing-fact abstention from 10/12 to 12/12 for the Huatuo-labeled checkpoint, but correct use of explicitly negative context falls from 12/12 to 2/12. For MedSIGHT, the same prompt improves missing-fact abstention from 6/12 to 12/12 but reduces correct anatomy under conflicting notes from 12/12 to 1/12. These are constrained choice-score results, not free-text clinical error rates.

Coarse head/chest anatomy is decodable and used in both checkpoints, including baseline decisions under conflicting notes. That is a useful negative result against a blanket coverage-gap story. It says nothing decisive about small lesions or unreported findings. The Huatuo-labeled local checkpoint has a LLaVA-Qwen2 architecture; do not silently equate it with the original 2024 HuatuoGPT-Vision-34B paper configuration.

Theory worth keeping, with narrower claims

Let Y be a finite finding label, I the complete supplied image input, C omitted context, and Z=g(I) a deterministic frozen representation. Hold the question fixed, or condition every term below on the question. With log base 2 and a common population distribution:

E[−log₂ q(Y|Z)]
= H(Y|I,C) + I(Y;C|I) + I(Y;I|Z)
+ EZ KL₂(p(Y|Z) || q(Y|Z)).

The identity follows from cross-entropy = conditional entropy + KL, then H(Y|Z) = H(Y|I) + I(Y;I|Z), then H(Y|I) = H(Y|I,C) + I(Y;C|I). Deterministic Z ensures the required conditional independence. If context is actually supplied, define the representation and conditioning accordingly. The decomposition is a population identity, not a per-record diagnosis of the model’s error.

The last term includes approximation, fitting and calibration error, rather than only a failure to look at retained evidence. Lost encoding is not identical to absent report coverage: input resizing, frame omission and representation compression can lose information about reported findings too. Reader disagreement belongs in H(Y|I,C) only if Y is the reader label or its noise affects the chosen target; it is not automatically biological irreducibility.

P(error) ≥ max{0, [H₂(Y|Z) − 1] / log₂ K}, K = |Y| ≥ 2.

This coarse Fano bound is valid for predictors restricted to frozen Z. It is often vacuous, especially for binary labels, and gives no useful numerical floor without estimating H(Y|Z). It does not prove a universal pretraining/post-training boundary. Updating the encoder or acquiring evidence changes the premise.

Ablation ≠ information estimation. A single model’s log q(y|I) − log q(y|no image) measures that model under a chosen intervention, which may be out of distribution. It can be negative even when true image information is positive. The archived synthetic theory check exhibits exactly that. Proper PVI uses specified predictor families, comparable fitted null/input predictors and held-out evaluation [T01]. Neither PVI nor a probe automatically assigns an expert evidence-sufficiency label.

Conformal calibration is a later layer. Choose the actual loss, calibration units and monotone/nested output family before invoking a theorem [T02–T03]. Standard expected-risk control is not per-patient certainty or automatically a guarantee among non-abstained cases. Clinical labels must distinguish missed findings, false findings and unsupported attribution; reports alone are insufficient. Hold calibration patients aside from score design and test external sites separately. Rare-finding or site-specific guarantees can require far more than a few hundred cases.

The decisive study to propose

Start with one modality and two evidence requirements: current-versus-prior CXR comparisons, and image-versus-pathology claims in PMC-derived VQA. Do not begin with broad pretraining, a learned information decomposition and conformal deployment guarantees simultaneously.

StageDesignWhat it can decide
1. Independent auditUniform samples across sources, not only keyword hits. Two qualified readers annotate atomic claims: visible, contextual, derived, unavailable, ambiguous; mark supporting view/timepoint and disagreement. Blind readers to model identity.Estimate claim- and example-level mismatch separately, with patient/article clustering and adjudicated intervals. Include visibly unreported findings to test the coverage hypothesis.
2. Factorial evidence testHold the question and current image fixed. Add/withhold the actual prior or pathology report; separately change irrelevant context. Use matched original image pairs and only validated lesion edits.Missing-evidence attribution versus legitimate context updating, rather than generic refusal. Supply provenance and authority so contradiction tests are well defined.
3. Matched training interventionSame records, tokens, steps, backbone and initialization: original targets; cleaned/provenance targets; original targets plus MCR-like objective; aligned targets plus that objective. Add a size-matched random-removal control.A causal effect of supervision alignment beyond data quantity, answer frequency or generic grounding rewards.
4. Representation interventionIndependently labeled lesion-present/absent data; matched acquisition/anatomy. Compare held-out probes at encoder/projector/LLM layers and actual decisions. Then contrast frozen versus updated encoder with controlled budgets.Locate a practical bottleneck. A failed finite probe alone cannot establish lost information, and a successful probe alone cannot establish causal lesion use.
5. GeneralizationSplit by patient and source article before generating QA. Freeze evaluation prompts, masks, annotation policy and model checkpoints. Reserve distinct calibration and external-test patients.Avoid near-duplicate figures, reference leakage, template memorization and tuning on the evaluation cases.

Primary outcome: joint evidential success

Count a case successful only when the model answers adequately with sufficient evidence, preserves the answer under an irrelevant intervention, removes or qualifies the affected claim when its evidence is withheld, and updates correctly when valid evidence arrives. Report these components separately as well. For ambiguous diagnoses use probabilistic targets or expert acceptable sets, rather than demanding a unique definitive label.

Measure unsupported claim rate, current-finding sensitivity, false-positive rate, relevant/irrelevant intervention response, evidence-acquisition choice, and risk versus coverage. Include the rate of correct final answer with a false or unavailable visual premise. Withholding an image needed for a question should not be scored identically to obtaining a negative image that supports “absent.” A no-lesion answer and insufficient evidence are different outputs.

Falsification and practical decision rules

  • If independent readers judge most sampled targets adequately supported, the broad mismatch-prevalence hypothesis weakens.
  • If aligned-target training does not improve held-out joint success beyond equal-size random cleaning or MCR-style training, the causal training claim weakens.
  • If gains come entirely from extra abstention with fewer correct answerable cases, the proposed mitigation fails.
  • If added valid context does not restore factual specificity, investigate context use and the uncertainty policy before adding pretraining.
  • If a stronger frozen readout or improved crops resolve the finding, do not attribute failure to irrevocably lost encoder information.
Advisor decision. This is ready as a scoped research hypothesis with traceable evidence. Ask the advisor to choose a modality, secure annotation expertise, and agree on the matched supervision intervention and primary joint metric. Present the coverage mechanism and the dominant-root-cause claim as open questions.

Files and reproduction

New artifacts are confined to this folder. The source datasets and pre-existing experiment outputs were not modified. The report embeds displayed images and plots for offline reading; source links require internet. The slides contain source IDs and speaker notes. Dataset use remains subject to each original source’s terms.

python -m pip install ijson numpy matplotlib pillow python-pptx pymupdf
python Plans/medical_mllm_gap_review/audit_data.py
python Plans/medical_mllm_gap_review/benchmark_text_baseline.py
python Plans/medical_mllm_gap_review/build_review.py

The selected case manifest and evidence catalog are curated inputs; rebuilding does not replace specialist adjudication. The audit stores a reproducible uniform reservoir and a separate set of screening examples. No model inference is performed by these commands.

  • Dataset counts, regexes and input SHA256 checksums
  • Baseline definitions, counts and intervals · Per-question predictions
  • Uniform PubMedVision reservoir, 4,000 records
  • Full curated examples with provenance

  • Review scope and source-note checksum
  • Existing mismatch pilot · Existing information-gap pilot

The existing pilot links above are available within the repository. Evidence strength: structural input availability is directly auditable; fine diagnostic sufficiency and causal training effects remain to be established.
